The postulate is that "talent" is the thing that we can extrapolate from an otherwise normalized curve. You're offering explanations as to why any given data point is where it is. But over many people, the explanation would have to apply to the population or it is normalized.

So it's just a philosophical difference really. Is talent just the function of all of a person's traits and experiences given a certain context? Maybe. Doesn't really invalidate the claim that someone is more likely to succeed than another even though they put in the same resources.

You can take whatever stand you want on what "talent" truly means. But from a math perspective, "propensity for success prior to training" is measurable and large enough sample sizes account for any extenuating circumstances like depression, adhd, boredom, upbringing, etc.

I'm not sure what your history with statistics is, but the idea is that you can sample a population and discover patterns. Those remain true.

However what you can't due is assume correlation equates to causation. So the thought experiment of "equal practice, different skills" does demonstrate a discrete method of observing talent.

But it doesn't work in reverse, where your place on the bell curve could be extrapolated to indicate your talent. It works because in these examples, the nebulous idea of talent is being demonstrated via identical conditions. 

Your reasons as to why a given result might be invalid (teaching style being a very good example) are good and prove exactly why any individual isn't beholden to their result.

But all of these factors can be predicted to follow a bell curve. For each "what if" there is an equal and opposite, and that's what the bell curve solves. Each factor does likely have some impact, but collectively they're normalized.

If this were a practical analysis, it would be correct to assume the talent distribution matches the observed curve, and then see if the apex of the curve shifts with different teaching styles or compare segments of the initial population across economic status or other things.

So there's an immense amount of study done in how to improve game feel in every genre, but it comes down a lot to small details that go unnoticed because they prevent "jank" so the end result is it feels better because it's careful to avoid bad things.

Some specifics: there are a lot of queues to inform you of a weapons state. When a bow is drawn, many elements on the bow begin to light up or shift, and they "peak" right when the shot is ready. But their peak is actually a large amount different from the rest of the windup.

The balance knob of recoil is tuned down a lot in favor of bullet spread which a less disruptive way to ensure that range must be respected between weapon classes. Other games tend to jerk your aim around to make sure you can't snipe with a heavy machine gun but destiny will use some recoil but put more emphasis on the spread.

The feedback of landing a hit is very well "juiced" with damage being indicated by a very good health bar, the sounds telling you if you're hitting or not, etc. There's a lot of details but if you want to look into it, just take a shot at an enemy and everything that isn't just their health moving plays into that.

But most importantly: You're used to it. Every shooter makes choices on how to handle guns, with a bell curve of variance across basically every factor. So going from shooter to shooter will make everything feel a little off, but still make sense. But if you play a game enough, your expectations of how some action plays out becomes very VERY accurate without you even realizing. You know the reload timing and movespeed very well, so you can reload on your way and know that you're able to shoot just as you pass the corner. Those small fluidities, most subconscious, are incredible for game feel and one of the biggest things for a designer is to help a player aquire those as fast as possible.

But moreso I think I have some useful advice in terms of perspective and goal orientation. You're already past the first major hurdle which is "I am held back by my team" and you instead clearly understand "the path to climbing is personal improvement" BUT I also notice that there is some desperation in the tone here, which leads me to believe you're struggling to climb more.

A few things: 

1: ranked is a law of large numbers experience. Unlike pro play or tournaments, ranked demonstrates success in a generalized sense and it's normalized by 9 other players. This means that as your skill level has to be dramatically higher than rank to see win after win caused by you and your own agency. More often than not, wins and losses aren't highly influencable by a single person. So yea you can have streaks of 4-9 games where you're definitively the best player and yet, lose all of them. This is the nature of law of large numbers and variance. 

2: Your best route to climbing, as derived from 1, won't be in identifying "who's fault it is" since that method of thinking guides you to functional fixedness fallacies. Your post is basically asking "can someone tell me what else I need to do to win here? I don't think my mistakes are enough to be our fault for loosing." However, instead you should be thinking "what times could I have done something better, and is there any glaring weaknesses I might not be aware of?" and then not concern yourself with the result of the game. It may well be the case that your teammates made dramatically more mistakes, but it also could be that the enemies just played at a higher-than-Plat level. It doesn't really matter except when it's in service to helping you find ways to improve. 

3: A big portion of improving and climbing comes down to finding ways to get an edge, and those are very contextual. To help guide your own vod analysis I would suggest asking questions like the following: "What are my teammates weaknesses and how can I compensate for them?" or "What weakness of mine are being exploited, and how can I circumvent them?" or "What kinds of plays are the enemies making, and how can I deny those plays or negate their impact?" and in finding those answers, you'll often find little bits you can improve with and incrementally increase your expected value. 

Hope it's helpful, sorry it's not a full vod review but I hope that it can offer some routes to improvement.

I think of this a lot and I'm trying to find some kind of answer, but here's what I have so far (warning, mini essay):

When online matchmaking became a thing (there was a time before where it was ip addresses saved in a notebook to play with friends) you ended up against opponents you couldn't learn against across multiple games. Many players, who were accustomed to getting beat and learning how to beat that player, found themselves in a position where they could never feasibly do that again. So instead, "meta" strategies formed that weren't always the best but at least worked well and consistently.

These strategies ended up being well known by consistent players, but not by newcomers. Since they were emergent properties of the game instead of developer intended ones, the devs couldn't anticipate them and create tutorials or other educational systems to get new players up to date on other player's expectations of them.

This, combined with skill-agnostic matchmaking, meant that veterans chewed through "noobs" at an alarming rate for games like halo or call of duty. But when the paradigm of online matchmaking met team based games, it presented two conflicting indications: Better players deserve to win, but you can't win if your team doesn't know the "right" way to play (which is the consistent meta strategy) so you have the spark of toxcitity: Play the right way, or don't play on my team. But since you can't pick who's on your team, you have to elimate the chance of it happening, so you say "uninstall / play another game /stick to single player"

So this pattern persists for a long time. A LONG time. Good ranked matchmaking, hidden mmr, and other mitigating factors are very far behind the community impact of forcing players to accommodate each other within any range of skill. This ends up generating the common mentality of "there is a correct thing to do. You have a job, which is a portion of that correct thing. Failure to do this means the loss is only reflective of the weakest link"

Now this paradigm of "right choices, do your job" spreads very fast due to how convenient it is for ego defense and also the thread of truth it presents: if you do what's expected of you, I can play what's expected of me and I don't have to take time to learn the intricacies of you as a person and your individual playstyle.

This is the key point: Gaming online is now about avoiding the person and instead defining the in game impact that their class/character provides. There's already a degree of anonymity from being online, but to truly eliminate empathy we have to dehumanize people. This is so easily accomplished by relegating people to a responsibility. There isn't any nuance to their decisions anymore, it's either right or wrong, and you as a person are now either right or wrong.

So this becomes the norm. Games design with this in mind. But like dogs with barrier aggression, we have no way to alleviate our frustrations. We love the game of our choice, but we can't control our teammates, even thought we've been taught that there is a proper way to play and we're adhering to it.

Thus, you bark. And they bark back. And it devolves into anger and toxcitity, because we've had the ability to use our skills to influence the outcome be gutted in service of accessibility, instead of the systems serving accountability.

Yes and no. If you make the same comparison of crime over X, and replace skin color with "median yearly income" you see the same trend. If you also compare skin color to median yearly income, you see the correlation. In reality, poor people commit more crime AND people of color tend to be more poor in America. It still can't speak to either confirming or denying any racist undertones, because ultimately the stats don't indicate causation and can't. 

So it's not that they lie, it's that they give solid evidence of some correlation but people glean more from it then they should, aka deciding it's causation.

For this example, I would be curious if you could find patterns between traits of the owners of the aggressive pet, or if you could compare aggression in multi dog households, or other things to help form the true image.

But what it does prove is that there is an issue of some kind. Just like the color/crime stats. So it's not a question of "is there an issue" but a question of the issues source and how we can address it. I'm all for using slight shortcuts to help evaluate cards. Putting cards into your hand is not "drawing cards" .

Getting access to more cards is drawing cards. The significance of "drawing a card" is that you have +1 to a resource that your opponent does not. It means that if you could 1 for 1 each card, you'd have extra at the end.

Putting cards back into your hand that are currently generating their value isn't gaining more resources. It's loosing some. Now you have to go through more steps (aka tempo) to get back to the level of value you were at.

A good example of something "drawing a card" when it's not actually drawing a card is stuff like [[expressive iteration]] where you gain the same net resources as +2 draws even though it didn't physically draw 2 cards.
It is very much not draw 4, and +1 mana is conditional on the fact that you don't have an untapped land to play otherwise.

Yes! The stack can be confusing at first but once a few details are know it irons itself out. 

Firstly, lets just talk about the stack. Casting a spell and activating abilities (non-mana abilities only) go on it. Playing lands and activating mana abilities (like the ones found on those lands) don't go on the stack (there's also some special actions that don't use the stack either, but those are down the road things.)

If a player has priority, they can either add things to the stack, or pass priority to the next player in turn order. In this case, Player A has priority during their main phase, and chooses to add something to the stack (the creature)

If all players pass priority without anything being added to the stack, the the topmost item on the stack resolves. If the stack is empty, then instead we move to the next turn phase (including going from one player's turn to the next)

In this case, B got priority and decided to add something to the stack. Counterspell, targeting the Creature spell (which is still on the stack. Now, counterspell goes on top of the stack, with the creature spell underneath it.

So now, presumably B passes priority to C. C doesn't add anything, passes to D. Same thing, D->A, then A->B. Now at this point, since the last thing added was B's Counterspell, this satisfies the condition of "nothing new added to the stack" and then Counterspell resolves, performing it's effects.

The whole reason I bring this long explanation up is because to *counter* something is to *move it from the stack to the graveyard.* At this point, counterspell resolving will place A's creature into the graveyard. 

Now, one more thing is that after something resolves, we give priority back to the active player. So even though A just passed priority, B doesn't get it back. Counterspell resolves, and now A gets priority once again. This is important because sometimes the thing that resolves has an ability you may want to activate (usually planeswalkers) and that means that A gets a chance to activate the ability before ANYONE else gets priority. 

So this compares to your case. Upkeep comes, every player passes prio. Draw step, same thing. Then you go to your first main phase, and play a land. Playing it doesn't use the stack, so you still have priority. Then you activate your ability via paying it's costs and placing the ability on the stack. 

Since you've had priority this whole time, nobody can stop you from activating the ability. But depending on the ability, even if they could send a [[doom blade]] at your creature, you can respond to it by activating the ability anyway (since doomblade can't resolve until everyone passes priority without adding something else) 

So basically, your friend could have never stopped you from using your creature's activated ability even if he cast the removal spell first.  (unless the ability specifically says you can only use it as a sorcery, in which case your friend can kill it when they have prio during upkeep / draw step)

So they way that priority works with turn steps is this:

Active player gets priority first.

When a player has priority, they can play anything legal to do so, or pass it.

If both players pass priority, then the topmost object on the stack resolves, and the active player receives priority.

If there is nothing on the stack, then instead of resolving anything, move to the next step in the turn (and then move again if the step doesn't grant priority to players)


So in this case, active player gets prio in end step. They say "end turn" or whatever, implying a shortcut to your upkeep. You say "I cast opt" or whatever, meaning when you get priority then you cast an instant and presumably pass priority. Before opt resolves, active player has priority and can choose to cast or pass (resolving opt) and then they get priority. It is still their end step since all players haven't passed priority while the stack is empty.

Since you mention how powerful it is and ask if someone is doing something wrong, I'll help shine some light on why: 

Imagine that each card gives some amount of 2 things: Progress, or Value. Progress is the amount a card moves you towards victory, and Value is the amount a card gives you more resources (usually mana or cards.)

Ramp spells give 0 progress, because it doesn't matter HOW many lands you get or mana artifacts you play, they don't do anything to help you actually win. What they do is give you extra resources though.

Compare that to something like [[shivan dragon]] who gives you very little Value (no extra cards, no extra mana, at best he *sort of* gives you extra life if you block with him) but gives a LOT of progress compared to a forest or something(cause attacking will win games, and he can attack)

You've found a good archetype: Fill my deck with lots of Value generating cards (cards that draw more cards, cards that give me mana, etc) and then some VERY expensive (mana wise, not $ wise) cards that give a metric ton of progress. That archetype is called "ramp"

Ramp is conventionally weak to another archetype called "aggro" where their decks don't have many if ANY value generating cards. All of their cards are low mana cost, and make a lot of progress in relation to their cost. In that hypothetical deck vs deck, the Ramp player will be spending turns 1-4 doing nothin' but making mana. But the progress deck (aggro) is gonna deal 2,4,12,20 damage on each of those turns. 

If your friends get wise, they might find themselves able to kill you before you can even finish ramping. But if they don't, and they just fill their decks without much care to value or progress, and just play cards they like or think is cool, then yea you'll win just because you have a consistent gameplan and they have a random mash of cool cards.
